intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1C gene (114205) on chromosome 12p13.33.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1C gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We expand the phenotype associated with CACNA1C variants to include neurodevelopmental abnormalities and epilepsy, in the absence of classic features of Timothy syndrome or long QT syndrome.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not state the chromosomal location. The claim counts as supported only because a gene's location is standard nomenclature restating the CACNA1C gene the paper names.

paragraphs.text: NEDHLSS is a mainly neurological disorder. Its features vary and include developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism, hypotonia, epilepsy, and ataxia. Affected individuals do not have significant cardiac manifestations or other features of Timothy syndrome. The phenotype differs broadly between individuals with truncating and nontruncating CACNA1C mutations (Rodan et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) described a girl (patient 1) of English/Ukrainian ancestry, born to nonconsanguineous parents, with neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy. Tonic and tonic-myoclonic seizures began within hours of birth and evolved into epileptic tonic spasms at 3 months. Multiple antiepileptic drugs failed to control the seizures, although clobazam reduced them. She had profound axial and appendicular hypotonia, no developmental progress at 18 months, inability to fixate or track visually, and severe sleep-wake disturbance. Other features were laryngomalacia, bilateral clubfeet, 3-4 finger and 2-3 toe syndactyly, camptodactyly, micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, frontal bossing, scant hair, inverted nipples, mild optic nerve hypoplasia, anal stenosis, and dysphagia that required a gastrostomy tube. EEG showed distinctive diffuse excessive fast activity. Brain MRI, echocardiogram, and Holter monitoring were normal.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) also described a family of Irish and German descent. The proband (patient 2), a girl, had tetralogy of Fallot, which was repaired at 2 months. At 4 months she developed severe biventricular failure with left ventricular noncompaction. She had mild dysmorphic features, including flat nasal bridge, low-set cupped ears, deep-set eyes, thin upper lip, and round face. She also had mild 2-3-4 toe syndactyly, mild developmental delay, and mild hypotonia. Her father (patient 3) had a congenital ventricular septal defect, aortic valve stenosis, learning disabilities, and ADHD. He developed focal-to-generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 18 years, and his craniofacial features were similar to his daughter's. Bozarth et al. (2018) noted that only 3 individuals with seizures and CACNA1C-related disorders had been reported before their series. They concluded that their findings extended the phenotype to neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy and late-onset epilepsy, and that this family showed variable expressivity. They suggested that CACNA1C be included on epilepsy gene panels.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) reported 25 individuals from 22 families with heterozygous CACNA1C mutations. Fourteen individuals had de novo nontruncating mutations, and all 14 had developmental delay or intellectual disability. At last follow-up, 9 were nonverbal and 6 were nonambulatory. One had a formal diagnosis of autism and 6 others had autistic features. Twelve were hypotonic and 4 had ataxia. Prenatal findings were reduced fetal movement (3 of 14), bilateral clubfoot (2 of 14), and oligohydramnios (2 of 14). The course was consistent with a static neurodevelopmental disorder. Brain MRI was normal apart from an incidental arachnoid cyst in 1 individual and prominent cerebellar folia in another. Ten of the 14 had epilepsy, with onset between 2 months and 8 years. Both generalized and focal epilepsies occurred, including West syndrome/infantile spasms, myoclonic seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Seizures were fever-sensitive in 3 individuals and medically refractory in 4, and EEG findings varied across the cohort. Twelve of the 14 had orthopedic abnormalities. Two had bilateral clubfoot with congenital finger contractures, and 2 others had persistently adducted thumbs. Other orthopedic findings were kyphosis or scoliosis (2 of 14), congenital hip dysplasia (3 of 14), syndactyly (2 of 14), and joint hypermobility (3 of 14). ECGs were obtained in 11 of these individuals, and 9 were normal. One individual (P13) had prolonged QT with T-wave alternans on Holter monitoring, and another had a possible ventricular conduction delay. Echocardiograms showed only minor findings, and no individual had the physical features of Timothy syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) performed patch clamp studies on several missense mutations. In HEK293 cells, the L1408V mutation reduced current density to about 30% of control without changing protein expression, consistent with loss of function. The L614P mutation caused modest current increases with a hyperpolarizing shift in activation, but the increase was not statistically significant. The authors described L614P as gain of function in the Results and as having a neutral effect in the Discussion. The L614R mutation, studied with CACNB2, caused no statistically significant change in current or gating.
